claim: During M phase, Endosulfine (Endos) family proteins are phosphorylated by Greatwall kinase (Gwl).
source: During M phase, Endosulfine (Endos) family proteins are phosphorylated by Greatwall kinase (Gwl), and the resultant pEndos inhibits the phosphatase PP2A-B55
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript

claim: Gwl-phosphorylated pEndos inhibits the phosphatase PP2A-B55.
source: During M phase, Endosulfine (Endos) family proteins are phosphorylated by Greatwall kinase (Gwl), and the resultant pEndos inhibits the phosphatase PP2A-B55
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: PP2A-B55 is the enzyme responsible for dephosphorylating pEndos during M phase exit.
source: We show here that PP2A-B55 is the enzyme responsible for dephosphorylating pEndos during M phase exit.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including depletion studies, purification, and kinetic analysis

claim: The kinetic parameters for PP2A-B55's action on pEndos are orders of magnitude lower than those for CDK-phosphorylated substrates.
source: The kinetic parameters for PP2A-B55's action on pEndos are orders of magnitude lower than those for CDK-phosphorylated substrates
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic measurements shown in Table 1 and Figure 7

claim: The Km for pEndos dephosphorylation by PP2A-B55 is approximately 1 nM.
source: Table 1 shows Km values of 0.47-1.0 nM for pEndos
evidence: Measured experimentally through kinetic analysis and okadaic acid competition experiments

claim: The Km for pCDKS dephosphorylation by PP2A-B55 is 71-99 μM.
source: Table 1 shows Km values of 71-99 μM for pCDKS
evidence: Measured experimentally through kinetic analysis

claim: The kcat for pEndos dephosphorylation by PP2A-B55 is 0.03-0.12 s⁻¹.
source: Table 1 shows kcat values of 0.03-0.12 s⁻¹ for pEndos
evidence: Measured experimentally through kinetic analysis

claim: The kcat for pCDKS dephosphorylation by PP2A-B55 is 22.5 s⁻¹.
source: Table 1 shows kcat value of 22.5 s⁻¹ for pCDKS
evidence: Measured experimentally through kinetic analysis

claim: Anti-Endos activity remains active during M phase while anti-CDKS activity is undetectable.
source: During M phase, anti-CDKS (light blue squares) is undetectable, whereas anti-Endos (light red circles) is active.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Xenopus CSF extracts as shown in Figure 2A

claim: Anti-CDKS activity is strongly induced as extracts exit M phase.
source: As the extracts exit M phase (interphase is achieved within 15–20 min of Ca2+ addition), anti-CDKS activity (dark blue squares) is strongly induced
evidence: Shown experimentally in Figure 2A with Ca2+-induced M phase exit

claim: Anti-Endos activity increases about twofold during M phase exit.
source: while anti-Endos (dark red circles) increases about twofold
evidence: Shown experimentally in Figure 2A

claim: Anti-Endos and anti-CDKS have similar sensitivities to okadaic acid.
source: Anti-Endos and anti-CDKS have similar sensitivities to okadaic acid and fostriecin
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Anti-Endos is substantially more resistant than anti-CDKS to tautomycetin.
source: but anti-Endos is substantially more resistant than anti-CDKS to tautomycetin and phosphomimetic Endos S68D
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: The IC50 for tautomycetin is approximately 10-fold higher for anti-Endos than for anti-CDKS.
source: The IC50 for tautomycetin (B–E) or tautomycin (F) is consistently ∼10-fold higher for anti-Endos than for anti-CDKS when measured in the same extract.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B-F

claim: Anti-Endos activity is insensitive to phosphomimetic Endos S68D while anti-CDKS is strongly inhibited.
source: Although anti-CDKS activity is strongly inhibited by phosphomimetic Endos (S68D), anti-Endos activity is insensitive to addition of this molecule.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: The specific activity of anti-CDKS increases upon dilution of the extract.
source: The specific activities of anti-CDKS and anti-H3 increase upon dilution of the extract, presumably because weakly binding inhibitors are titrated away
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: The specific activity of anti-Endos increases at most only marginally upon dilution.
source: but the specific activity of anti-Endos increases at most only marginally upon dilution
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: All anti-Endos activity is suppressed by relatively low doses of okadaic acid or calyculin A.
source: All of the activity in all extracts tested was suppressed by relatively low doses of okadaic acid or calyculin A
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Anti-Endos activity is completely resistant to the calcineurin (PP2B) inhibitor cyclosporin A.
source: but was completely resistant to the calcineurin (PP2B) inhibitor cyclosporin A (data not shown)
evidence: Stated as experimental result

claim: The enzyme(s) targeting the Gwl site in Endos belong to the PPP family of phospho-serine/threonine protein phosphatases.
source: These results indicate that the enzyme(s) targeting the Gwl site in Endos belong to the PPP family of phospho-serine/threonine protein phosphatases, which include PP1, PP2A, PP4, PP5, and PP6
evidence: Inferred from okadaic acid and calyculin A sensitivity patterns

claim: The majority of anti-Endos activity (70-90%) is sensitive to fostriecin.
source: The predominant anti-Endos activity in many cell types (∼70–90% of the total depending on the experiment) is thus due to PP2A, PP4, or PP6.
evidence: Determined from fostriecin sensitivity experiments shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: PP1 and PP5 are approximately 10,000-fold more resistant to fostriecin than the PP2A/PP4/PP6 group of enzymes.
source: PP1 and PP5 are ∼10,000-fold more resistant to the inhibitor fostriecin than the PP2A/PP4/PP6 group of enzymes
evidence: Cited from Swingle et al., 2007

claim: A minor fraction of anti-Endos is fostriecin-resistant and labile.
source: A minor fraction of anti-Endos is nonetheless fostriecin-resistant; this part of the activity is labile and is seen in some extract preparations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C,F) but not others
evidence: Shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Depletion of PP2A-A or PP2A-C from S2 tissue culture cells removes most anti-Endos from extracts.
source: The data indicate that a form of PP2A is responsible for about 90% of anti-CDKS, ∼70 to 80% of anti-Endos
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A with RNAi depletion experiments

claim: Treatment of HeLa cells with siRNA to the PP4 catalytic subunit does not affect anti-Endos levels.
source: Treatment of HeLa cells with siRNA to the PP4 catalytic subunit strongly reduces the amount of PP4 but does not obviously affect anti-Endos levels.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: No obvious changes in anti-Endos levels are seen in mutant mouse MEF cells homozygous for a null mutation in the gene encoding the PP5 catalytic subunit.
source: No obvious changes in anti-Endos levels are seen in the mutant mouse MEF cells homozygous for a null mutation in the gene encoding the PP5 catalytic subunit
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: Drosophila larvae lacking B55 (twins mutants) are severely deficient in anti-Endos activity.
source: Levels of anti-Endos are much lower in twins (encoding the sole B55 subunit in Drosophila) larvae than in wild-type (WT) controls (p<10−20; Student's two-tailed t test)
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A with statistical analysis

claim: Drosophila larvae lacking B55 are also severely deficient in anti-CDKS activity.
source: this is also the case as expected for anti-CDKS (p<1010)
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A with statistical analysis

claim: Phosphatase activity against Histone H1v1.0 is relatively unaffected in twins mutant larvae.
source: As a control, phosphatase activity against Histone H1v1.10 is relatively unaffected in twins mutant larvae.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A

claim: No consistent effects on anti-Endos were observed in extracts from larvae mutant for genes encoding other phosphatase subunits (B56, B‴, PP4R3, PP1 catalytic subunits).
source: No consistent effects were observed in extracts made from larvae mutant for genes encoding the other phosphatase subunits indicated, with two exceptions.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A

claim: Anti-Endos activity co-purifies with anti-CDKS activity during Mono-Q chromatography.
source: anti-Endos copurifies with the anti-CDKS activity previously ascribed to PP2A-B55 heterotrimer
evidence: Shown in Figure 5 where both activities peak in the same fractions

claim: Anti-Endos activity co-fractionates with PP2A-A, PP2A-C, and B55 subunits during Mono-Q chromatography.
source: Figure 5 shows Western blots indicating that PP2A-A, PP2A-C, and B55 subunits co-fractionate with anti-Endos and anti-CDKS activities
evidence: Shown in Figure 5 Western blots

claim: PP2A-B55α and PP2A-B55δ heterotrimers efficiently dephosphorylate Gwl-phosphorylated Endos.
source: PP2A-B55α and PP2A-B55δ heterotrimers showed similar strong levels of activity against all three substrates
evidence: Shown in Figure 6A with purified recombinant enzymes

claim: PP2A-B56β heterotrimers fail to dephosphorylate Gwl-phosphorylated pEndos.
source: PP2A-B56β heterotrimers and PP2A-A/C heterodimers, both of which dephosphorylated the generic MyBP substrate, failed to dephosphorylate either Gwl-phosphorylated pEndos or the pCDKS substrate.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6A

claim: PP2A-A/C heterodimers fail to dephosphorylate Gwl-phosphorylated pEndos.
source: PP2A-B56β heterotrimers and PP2A-A/C heterodimers, both of which dephosphorylated the generic MyBP substrate, failed to dephosphorylate either Gwl-phosphorylated pEndos or the pCDKS substrate.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6A

claim: The anti-Endos activity of purified PP2A-B55α heterotrimers has the same characteristics as the predominant anti-Endos activity in whole cell extracts.
source: The anti-Endos activity of purified PP2A-B55α heterotrimers has the same characteristics as the predominant anti-Endos activity in whole cell extracts.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing inhibitor sensitivities in Figure 6B-D with those in Figure 2

claim: Purified PP2A-B55 displays similar dose responses to fostriecin for both anti-Endos and anti-CDKS activities.
source: It is nonetheless clear that both the anti-Endos and anti-CDKS functions of PP2A-B555α display similar dose responses to this drug.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6D

claim: Thiophosphorylated Endos is a much stronger inhibitor of PP2A-B55 than unphosphorylated Endos.
source: Thiophosphorylation by Gwl kinase makes Endos into a much stronger inhibitor of PP2A-B55 than unphosphorylated Endos
evidence: Shown in Figure 8A comparing dose-response curves

claim: The affinity of thiophosphorylated Endos for PP2A-B55 is only about twofold lower than that of okadaic acid.
source: the affinity of thiophosphorylated Endos is only about twofold lower than that of okadaic acid
evidence: Shown in Figure 8A comparing IC50 values

claim: Non-radioactive pEndos is a less efficient inhibitor of PP2A-B55 than thiophosphorylated Endos because the enzyme dephosphorylates pEndos during incubation.
source: Non-radioactive pEndos is a less efficient inhibitor of PP2A-B55 than is thiophosphorylated Endos because the enzyme dephosphorylates pEndos during the course of incubation
evidence: Shown in Figure 8A and explained by the time-dependent shift in inhibition curves

claim: PP2A-B55 cannot recognize pCDKS substrate until the majority of pEndos in the same reaction has been dephosphorylated.
source: PP2A-B55 cannot recognize the pCDKS substrate until the majority of the pEndos in the same tube has been dephosphorylated.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 8A by comparing inhibition at different time points

claim: PP2A-B55 can auto-reactivate by dephosphorylating pEndos inhibitor.
source: A clear delay in pCDKS dephosphorylation of roughly 35 min is visible in the sample containing pEndos, after which the rate of the reaction approaches the initial rate observed in the absence of Endos inhibitors.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 8B showing time-dependent reactivation

claim: pEndos interacts with the active site of PP2A-B55.
source: Two findings clearly indicate that pEndos interacts with the active site of PP2A-B55. First, pEndos is a substrate that is dephosphorylated by this enzyme at a measurable rate; and second, pEndos competes with okadaic acid, a drug known to bind only to PP2A's active site
evidence: Based on substrate dephosphorylation and okadaic acid competition experiments

claim: pEndos does not inhibit PP2A-B55 by binding to a second, allosteric site separate from the active site.
source: Our results provide no indication that pEndos inhibits PP2A-B55 by binding to a second, allosteric site separate from the active site at which it is dephosphorylated.
evidence: Based on the observation that pEndos dephosphorylation rate does not decrease at high substrate concentrations (Figure 7B)

claim: The intracellular concentration of PP2A B55 subunit is between 100 and 250 nM.
source: From our own quantitation on Western blots, we estimate the intracellular concentration of the PP2A B55 subunit to be between 100 and 250 nM
evidence: Estimated from Western blot quantitation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6

claim: The intracellular concentration of Endos is between 500 nM and 1 μM.
source: and that of Endos to be between 500 nM and 1 μΜ, depending on the cell type
evidence: Estimated from Western blot quantitation

claim: The ratio of Endos to PP2A-B55 is approximately 5:1.
source: The 5:1 ratio of Endos to PP2A-B55 observed in that figure is roughly consistent with estimates from other laboratories
evidence: Shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6 and consistent with mass spectrometry data

claim: Approximately 50% of total Endos protein is phosphorylated during M phase in synchronized mammalian tissue culture cells.
source: other investigators have found that this proportion is roughly 50% in extracts of synchronized mammalian tissue culture cells
evidence: Cited from Cundell et al., 2013

claim: Approximately 100% of Endos is phosphorylated in frog egg M phase extracts.
source: and approaches 100% in frog egg M phase extracts
evidence: Cited from Mochida et al., 2010

claim: M phase exit is completed within less than 5 minutes in Xenopus cycling extracts.
source: M phase exit is surprisingly rapid given the large number of phosphorylations which must be reversed; in Xenopus cycling extracts, for example, the M phase-to-interphase transition is completed within less than 5 min
evidence: Cited from Zhao et al., 2008 and Mochida et al., 2009

claim: Half of PP2A-B55 is released from pEndos sequestration within 74 seconds after Gwl inactivation under physiological conditions.
source: Beyond this point, PP2A-B55 is rapidly released from sequestration; half is available to act on other substrates within 74 s
evidence: Calculated from mathematical modeling shown in Figure 10A

claim: Cells would be unable to exit M phase in a timely manner unless pEndos was dephosphorylated by PP2A-B55.
source: Further dynamic modeling surprisingly revealed a key insight: cells would be unable to exit M phase in a timely manner unless pEndos was in fact dephosphorylated by PP2A-B55 as demanded by unfair competition.
evidence: Demonstrated by mathematical modeling in Figure 10C,D showing that many hours would be required for M phase exit if pEndos were only an inhibitor

claim: If pEndos were only an inhibitor and not a substrate of PP2A-B55, many hours would be required for PP2A-B55 desequestration and M phase exit.
source: In this scenario, PP2A-B55 would protect the bound pEndos from dephosphorylation, so many hours—not just a few minutes—would be required for PP2A-B55 desequestration and M phase exit.
evidence: Shown by mathematical modeling in Figure 10C,D

claim: The dephosphorylation of pEndos by PP2A-B55 is an absolute requirement for rapid completion of the M phase-to-interphase transition.
source: In other words, the dephosphorylation of pEndos by PP2A-B55 is an absolute requirement for rapid completion of the M phase-to-interphase transition.
evidence: Concluded from mathematical modeling comparing scenarios in Figure 10

claim: A phosphatase other than PP2A-B55 must inactivate Gwl during M phase exit.
source: The obvious resolution of this dilemma is therefore that a phosphatase other than PP2A-B55 inactivates Gwl during M phase exit.
evidence: Inferred from the logic that PP2A-B55 cannot be the Gwl-inactivating phosphatase because the system would be futile

claim: Purified PP2A-B55 is very inefficient in inactivating Gwl in vitro.
source: First, in our hands purified PP2A-B55 in vitro is very inefficient in inactivating Gwl.
evidence: Stated as preliminary experimental result (data not shown)

claim: Active Gwl becomes rapidly inactivated and dephosphorylated in interphase extracts in a process that is insensitive to okadaic acid.
source: Second, when active Gwl is added to interphase extracts from a variety of cell types, it becomes rapidly inactivated and dephosphorylated in a process that is insensitive to okadaic acid
evidence: Stated as preliminary experimental result (data not shown)

claim: The identity of the Gwl-inactivating enzyme is currently unknown.
source: the identity of this Gwl-inactivating enzyme is currently unknown
evidence: Stated explicitly as a gap in current knowledge

claim: Depletion of Fcp1 does not decrease anti-Endos activity.
source: RNAi depletion of more than 90% of the Fcp1 in Drosophila S2 cells has no obvious effect on the ability of extracts made from these cells to dephosphorylate pEndos
evidence: Shown in Figure 11A,B

claim: Purified S. pombe Fcp1 enzyme has detectable but very low anti-Endos activity.
source: Purified S. pombe Fcp1 enzyme has detectable anti-Endos activity, but this is very low.
evidence: Shown in Figure 11C,D

claim: Each molecule of Fcp1 has less than 1/1,000th the efficiency of a molecule of PP2A-B55 in dephosphorylating pEndos at physiological substrate concentration.
source: At a physiological concentration of the pEndos (1 μM), each molecule of Fcp1 has less than 1/1,000th the efficiency of a molecule of PP2A-B55 in dephosphorylating this substrate
evidence: Calculated from data in Figure 11C,D

claim: Less than 0.01% of the total anti-Endos activity in cells can be ascribed to Fcp1.
source: By this estimate, less than 0.01% of the total anti-Endos activity in cells can be ascribed to Fcp1.
evidence: Calculated from enzyme efficiency and relative protein abundances

claim: Fcp1 does not co-fractionate with pEndos-dephosphorylating activity during mono-Q chromatography.
source: In mono-Q chromatography, Fcp1 does not co-fractionate with the pEndos-dephosphorylating activity. Figure 5 shows that fractions with peak anti-Endos activity (such as fractions from 37 to 39) have no detectable Fcp1 protein.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5

claim: PP1 could dephosphorylate PKA-phosphorylated Inhibitor-1 with Km and kcat values both considerably lower than for dephosphorylation of phosphorylase a.
source: The investigators found that purified PP1 could dephosphorylate PKA-phosphorylated Inhibitor-1, and the values of Km and kcat were both considerably lower for this reaction than for dephosphorylation of the more normal substrate phosphorylase a
evidence: Cited from Foulkes et al., 1983

claim: pInhibitor-1 acts both as an inhibitor and a substrate for PP1.
source: In short, just as we report here for pEndos and PP2A-B55, they concluded that pInhibitor-1 acts both as an inhibitor and a substrate for PP1.
evidence: Cited from Foulkes et al., 1983

claim: Entry of cells into M phase requires the phosphorylation of thousands of sites on hundreds of proteins.
source: Entry of cells into M phase of mitosis or meiosis requires the phosphorylation of thousands of sites on hundreds of proteins
evidence: Cited from multiple sources (Dephoure et al., 2008; Lindqvist et al., 2009; Dulla et al., 2010; Olsen et al., 2010)

claim: Many M phase phosphorylation sites are substrates of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs).
source: Many of these sites are substrates of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), most notably MPF (M phase-promoting factor; CDK1-Cyclin B).
evidence: Cited from Nigg, 1993 and Holmes and Solomon, 1996

claim: CDK phosphosites are 'proline-directed', being phosphorylated at serine or threonine followed by proline.
source: CDK phosphosites are 'proline-directed', being phosphorylated at serine or threonine followed by proline
evidence: Cited from Nigg, 1993 and Holmes and Solomon, 1996

claim: PP2A-B55 is the phosphatase responsible for removing many key CDK-generated phosphorylations at the conclusion of M phase.
source: PP2A-B55 (heterotrimeric protein phosphatase 2A composed of a catalytic C subunit, a structural A subunit, and a B55-type regulatory subunit) is the phosphatase responsible for removing many key CDK-generated phosphorylations at the conclusion of M phase
evidence: Cited from multiple sources (Clarke et al., 1993; Mayer-Jaekel et al., 1994; Mochida and Hunt, 2007; Castilho et al., 2009; Mochida et al., 2009; Schmitz et al., 2010)

claim: PP2A-B55 activity must be downregulated when cells go into M phase.
source: The circuitry's basic logic suggests that PP2A-B55 activity must be downregulated when cells go into M phase; if not, the phosphorylations catalyzed by MPF would be prematurely removed, preventing M phase entry
evidence: Logical inference from the regulatory circuit shown in Figure 1

claim: MPF phosphorylates Greatwall (Gwl) kinase.
source: One such MPF substrate is the kinase Greatwall (Gwl), which in its active form phosphorylates Endosulfine (Endos).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1 and cited from literature

claim: Phosphorylated Endos binds to and inhibits the phosphatase PP2A-B55.
source: Phosphorylated Endos binds to and inhibits the phosphatase PP2A-B55.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1 and cited from literature

claim: Inhibition of PP2A-B55 by pEndos protects MPF substrates from premature dephosphorylation during M phase entry.
source: This inhibition protects MPF substrates, including components of the autoregulatory loop, from premature dephosphorylation during M phase entry.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1 and based on established knowledge

claim: MPF is inactivated by degradation of its Cyclin B component during M phase exit.
source: During M phase exit, MPF is inactivated by degradation of its Cyclin B component (not shown)
evidence: Stated in Figure 1 legend and based on established knowledge

claim: PP2A-B55 becomes reactivated during M phase exit to dephosphorylate many MPF substrates.
source: and PP2A-B55 becomes reactivated to dephosphorylate many MPF substrates
evidence: Shown in Figure 1 and based on established knowledge

claim: M phase exit requires the dephosphorylation and inactivation of both Gwl and Endos.
source: M phase exit also requires the dephosphorylation and inactivation of both Gwl and Endos.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1 and based on logical inference

claim: If Gwl were to remain active, PP2A-B55 would stay inactive and the system would remain in M phase.
source: If Gwl were to remain active, it would continually keep Endos phosphorylated; PP2A-B55 would stay inactive and the system would remain in M phase because mitotic phosphorylations could not be removed.
evidence: Logical inference from the regulatory circuit

claim: If Gwl alone were inactivated but pEndos were to stay phosphorylated, M phase would be maintained.
source: On the other hand, if Gwl alone were inactivated but pEndos were to stay phosphorylated, M phase would again be maintained.
evidence: Logical inference from the regulatory circuit

claim: Most PP2A activity in vivo is ascribed to heterotrimeric enzymes containing the C and A subunits plus one of several kinds of regulatory B subunits.
source: Most PP2A activity in vivo is ascribed to heterotrimeric enzymes containing the C and A subunits plus one of several kinds of regulatory B subunits
evidence: Cited from Janssens et al., 2008

claim: The Drosophila genome has one B55-type PP2A regulatory subunit gene.
source: the Drosophila genome has a near-minimal set of genes encoding PP2A regulatory subunits (e.g., one B55-type subunit as opposed to four in mammals
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The Drosophila genome has two B56-class PP2A regulatory subunit genes.
source: and two B56-class [B′] subunits vs five in mammals
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Mammals have four B55-type PP2A regulatory subunit genes.
source: one B55-type subunit as opposed to four in mammals
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Mammals have five B56-class PP2A regulatory subunit genes.
source: and two B56-class [B′] subunits vs five in mammals
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The stabilities of the PP2A-A and PP2A-C subunits are mutually interdependent.
source: As reported elsewhere (Kamibayashi et al., 1992), the stabilities of the PP2A-A and PP2A-C subunits are mutually interdependent.
evidence: Cited from Kamibayashi et al., 1992 and shown in Figure 3B

claim: Gwl-phosphorylated pEndos inhibits PP2A-B55 dephosphorylation of CDK-phosphorylated substrates through competition for the active site.
source: These results suggest that Gwl-phosphorylated pEndos inhibits the dephosphorylation of CDK-phosphorylated substrates through competition for PP2A-B55's active site
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and illustrated in Figure 9

claim: During M phase, pEndos is in stoichiometric excess of PP2A-B55.
source: During M phase, pEndos is in stoichiometric excess of PP2A-B55, so due to the disparities in the kinetic constants of these substrates, almost all of the enzyme will accumulate as a tight-binding complex with pEndos.
evidence: Based on Western blot quantitation and mass spectrometry data

claim: Almost all PP2A-B55 accumulates as a tight-binding complex with pEndos during M phase.
source: so due to the disparities in the kinetic constants of these substrates, almost all of the enzyme will accumulate as a tight-binding complex with pEndos
evidence: Inferred from kinetic parameters and stoichiometry, illustrated in Figure 9

claim: PP2A-B55 can slowly dephosphorylate pEndos during M phase, but the inhibitor is replenished by action of Gwl.
source: Although PP2A-B55 can slowly dephosphorylate pEndos, the inhibitor is replenished by action of Gwl until this kinase is inactivated at anaphase onset
evidence: Shown in Figure 9 and based on experimental data

claim: When Gwl is inactivated, pEndos dephosphorylated by PP2A-B55 cannot be replaced.
source: When Gwl is inactivated during the M phase-to-interphase transition, the dynamic balance changes: pEndos dephosphorylated by PP2A-B55 cannot be replaced
evidence: Logical inference from the regulatory mechanism

claim: After Gwl inactivation, PP2A-B55 can refocus its attention on CDK-phosphorylated substrates.
source: so the phosphatase can refocus its attention on CDK-phosphorylated substrates
evidence: Logical inference from the inhibition by unfair competition mechanism

claim: The inhibition by unfair competition mechanism explains simultaneously how PP2A-B55 and Gwl together regulate pEndos, and how pEndos controls PP2A-B55.
source: This mechanism explains simultaneously how PP2A-B55 and Gwl together regulate pEndos, and how pEndos controls PP2A-B55.
evidence: Stated as the main conclusion of the study
